big_idea: If we share fairly, each group has the same amount.
learning_intention: We are learning to solve equal-group problems with totals up to 10, including problems where each group is a half.
student_learning_goal: I can solve equal-group problems with totals up to 10, including problems where each group is a half.
success_criteria: I can share a small collection fairly into 2 or more equal groups.
I can solve a half-group problem by splitting one item into two equal pieces.
I can draw a picture and write a number to show my equal-group share.
lesson_specific_materials: Adding Machine anchor poster — referenced from Lessons 1-4

OPTIONAL: Plus the Pup and Minnie the Mouse — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.
Per-group set of paper cookies (~30 in chocolate chip / oatmeal / sugar varieties; ~6 pre-cut along a half-line)
An anchor chart 'Equal Groups' with two columns: Whole Shares and Half Shares
Lesson 5 summative worksheet — provided in worksheet stage

minds_on.hook: Plus is having a birthday party with 4 friends. He has 8 cookies. How can he share fairly?
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Plus the Pup the puppet in hand, with a small basket of paper cookies. 'Friends — Plus is having a BIRTHDAY PARTY. He invited 4 friends. And he has 8 cookies. How does he share fairly?'

Lay out 4 paper plates in a row. 'Four friends — four plates. Watch.' Deal cookies one at a time, plate by plate: 1, 2, 3, 4. 'One round.' Continue: 5, 6, 7, 8. 'Two rounds.' Pause. 'How many cookies on each plate?' '2!' 'Right. Each friend gets 2 cookies. That's an EQUAL GROUP share. 8 cookies, 4 friends, 2 cookies each.'

Write on the chart: 8 ÷ 4 = 2 (using a fair-share notation friendly to Grade 1 — the explicit division symbol can wait, but the conceptual move is here). Or use a tape diagram with 4 boxes labeled 2 each, total 8.

Now the half-group reveal. 'But wait — what if Plus only has 5 cookies, and 2 friends are coming? How does he share fairly?' Set out 2 plates. Place 2 cookies on each plate. 'OK — 2 each. But wait — there's 1 cookie LEFT.' Hold up the leftover cookie. 'Hmm. We can't just put it on one plate — that wouldn't be fair. What can Plus do?'

Wait. Often a child says 'cut it in half!' 'YES — exactly. Plus can CUT the last cookie in HALF and give one half to each friend.' Demonstrate with a pre-cut paper cookie. Place one half on each plate. 'Now both friends have 2 AND A HALF cookies. That's still a fair share — each plate has the SAME amount.'

Write on the chart: 5 cookies, 2 friends, each gets 2½. 'Sometimes the answer is a whole number. Sometimes the answer is a half. Both are fair shares — as long as each group has the SAME amount.'

'Today we'll practice equal-group sharing with lots of small collections. Some will share evenly. Some will need a HALF.'
student_actions: Watch Plus deal cookies fairly to 4 friends.
Help count the cookies per plate.
Predict what to do when 5 cookies must share between 2 friends.
Echo the half-share solution: cut one cookie in half.

steps.instruction: Whole group: model 2 more equal-group problems together. Problem 1 (whole shares): 'Plus has 10 cookies and 5 friends are coming. Fair share?' Children predict 2 each, then verify by dealing. Problem 2 (half shares): 'Plus has 7 cookies and 2 friends. Fair share?' Children deal 3 each, then split the last cookie in half — 3½ each.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Two more sharing problems together. Predict first, then check by dealing onto plates. Listen for which problems need a HALF.' For Problem 2 explicitly slow down at the moment the leftover cookie appears — that's where the half-strategy gets named.

steps.instruction: Send pairs to three stations (~7 minutes each). Station A: Even Shares — pair has 4 sharing scenarios (8÷2, 6÷3, 10÷5, 8÷4). All have whole-number answers. Pair deals onto plates and writes the share. Station B: Half Shares — pair has 4 scenarios (5÷2, 7÷2, 3÷2, 9÷2). All require a half. Pair deals, splits the leftover, writes the share. Station C: Sort the Stories — pair has 8 story cards. Sort into 'Whole Share' and 'Half Share' piles. For each, identify how many friends and how many items.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Three stations, 7 minutes each. Some shares are EVEN — every plate gets the same whole number. Some shares need a HALF — one item gets split.' Set the rotation.

steps.instruction: Stretch challenge at Station C: include 2 cards that don't fit either pile — e.g., 7÷3 (which would need a third or two-thirds, beyond Grade 1). Pairs notice and discuss. Affirm: 'These shares need MORE than a half — that's a job for next year. For now, we can fair-share into 2 friends with halves, or any number of friends with WHOLES.'
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to pairs at Station C: 'You'll find some cards that don't fit. Why?' Lead pairs to notice that NOT EVERY share needs a half. Some need thirds or fourths. Star this on the chart as a Grade-2 preview.

steps.instruction: Circulate to record summative evidence on the Lesson 5 worksheet (administered after rotations) and observation evidence on the equal-group tracker. Watch for: (a) does the child correctly identify when a half is needed? (b) does the child split fairly (each friend gets EXACTLY the same)? (c) can the child write a sentence describing the share?
steps.teacher_prompt: Stop at each pair. Ask 'Does this share need a half? How do you know?' before checking their work. Mark the tracker.

differentiation.for_emerging: Children whose Lesson 1-4 fluency is still emerging stay at Station A (Even Shares) for both rotations. The half concept can be introduced separately in a small group later in the week. Build the equal-group concept on whole shares first.
differentiation.for_extending: Stretch story cards: include some 4-friend share scenarios where a half is needed (e.g., 6÷4 = 1½). These require splitting 2 cookies into halves, distributed across 4 friends. Pushes the half-share concept to its logical edge before Grade 2.
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Provide a sentence frame: 'There are ___ cookies and ___ friends. Each friend gets ___ cookies.' Provide picture-supported scenario cards. Pair with a strong-counter peer for Station B (the half-share station).
differentiation.for_movement_learners: Dealing physical cookies onto plates is naturally kinesthetic. For movement learners, allow them to BE the teacher — physically dealing one cookie to each child in a group. The motor act of one-per-plate is the embodied form of equal-group share.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: (1) does the child deal fairly (one-per-plate, then repeat) instead of clumping? (2) does the child correctly identify when a leftover needs to be split into halves? (3) can the child write a sentence describing the share? Children at L4 do all three; children at L3 deal fairly but don't yet handle halves cleanly.
formative_check.how_to_record: Tick the equal-group tracker per child as you observe. The Lesson 5 worksheet captures the summative version of the same evidence.
tracker_columns: Splits the leftover cleanly into halves

discussion_prompts: What's the rule for FAIR SHARES?
When does Plus need to cut a cookie in half?
If Plus has 6 cookies and 4 friends, can everyone get a whole? Why or why not?
What was the most fun way to share today — even shares or half shares?
consolidation.exit_routine: Each child draws their favourite share scenario from today on a sticky note (e.g., '5 cookies, 2 friends, 2½ each') and posts it on the Adding Machine anchor poster on the way to the door. End-of-unit certificate ceremony: each child receives a 'Junior Adding Machine Operator' certificate as part of the closing routine.

assessment_in_this_lesson.evidence_collected: Equal-group share with whole-number quotients, equal-group share with half quotients, and child-explained reasoning across the 4-prompt summative worksheet plus 3-5 station observations per child.
assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: Lesson 5 captures the B2.5 summative for the unit. Combined with Lessons 1-4 formative trackers, the teacher has evidence for all five expectations B2.1-B2.5: facts to 10 (Lesson 1), mental strategies to 20 (Lesson 2), addition-subtraction relationship and subtraction facts (Lesson 3), modelling story problems to 50 (Lesson 4), and equal-group sharing including halves (Lesson 5).

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child deals 5 cookies among 2 friends as 2 each with 1 leftover and stops there — repairing the 'fair share with leftover' vs. 'fair share by splitting' distinction
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
The most common Grade-1 trap on B2.5 (equal-group with halves) is the child who applies their Kindergarten fair-share strategy and STOPS at 'each friend gets 2, with 1 leftover'. This is fair WITH REMAINDER — a perfectly valid concept. But B2.5 specifically asks for fair shares EQUAL — each friend gets exactly the same amount. The leftover cookie must be split. The child's K-stage answer is right for K but wrong for Grade 1.

The distinction matters because B2.5's 'including problems in which each group is a half' is the entry point for fractional thinking. A child who gets to 'each friend gets 2, with 1 left over' is at the K boundary. A child who says 'cut the last one in half — each friend gets 2 and a half' has crossed into Grade 1's fair-share-with-halves territory. The expanded walkthrough covers the precise moment when a child stops at 'with remainder' and the teacher needs to push them to the half-share solution.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair is at Station B (Half Shares). The card reads 'Lila has 5 cookies. She wants to share them fairly between herself and Otto.' The child has dealt 2 cookies onto each plate. The child has set the 5th cookie to the side. They are looking at the teacher with a satisfied expression. Their answer: '2 each, 1 left over.'
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch beside the child. 'Tell me about your share.' The child says '2 each, 1 left over.' 'OK — both friends have 2 cookies each. Is that EQUAL?' 'Yes.' 'Does each friend have the SAME amount?' 'Yes — 2 each.' Pause. 'But there's still ONE cookie. What happens to it?' The child says 'It's leftover.' 'If Lila keeps it, who has more — Lila or Otto?' Wait. The child realises: 'Lila.' 'So is it STILL a fair share?' '... no.' 'Right. We can't just leave one over. We need to make it FAIR.'

Now the move. 'Watch what we can do.' Pick up the leftover cookie — ideally a pre-cut paper cookie that splits along a half-line. 'I cut this cookie in HALF.' Hold up both halves. 'One half for Lila — one half for Otto.' Place each half on the appropriate plate. 'Now look at each plate. How many WHOLE cookies on each plate?' '2.' 'And each plate also has…?' 'Half a cookie.' 'So each friend has 2 AND A HALF cookies. Same amount on each plate. That's a FAIR share.'

Let the child redo a few half-share problems independently. 7÷2 (3½ each), 9÷2 (4½ each). Watch for whether they automatically reach for the cut-in-half move. Tick 'identifies when half is needed' and 'splits cleanly' on the tracker.

If the child STILL stops at 'with leftover' after the demo: the half concept hasn't landed. Repair by going to the body. 'Put your hands flat in front of you.' Have the child clap once. 'One whole clap. Now — clap HALF a clap.' The child claps softly or barely. 'YES — that's HALF. Half is the same shape, just smaller. Now look at the cookie — same shape, just smaller.' Physical analogy can break the cognitive logjam.

Long-term recovery: introduce the half-share habit on Day 1 of the next unit's warm-up. Five minutes of cookie-style problems daily for two weeks moves most children from 'fair share with leftover' to 'fair share with half'.
expected_student_responses: (Confused) Stops at 'fair share with leftover'. Doesn't yet recognise that a leftover breaks the equal-group rule. Most common at the start of Grade 1 for transition learners; correct for K.
(Mid) Cuts the leftover when prompted but doesn't volunteer the move. Recognises the half-share once shown but doesn't see it as the natural extension of fair-sharing.
(Strong) Cuts the leftover automatically. Says 'I'll cut the last one in half so each friend gets 2 and a half.' Has internalised the half as a fair-share tool.

(Stretched) Volunteers an alternative split: 'I could cut both extra cookies into halves and give 4 halves to one friend and 4 halves to the other.' Sees that fair share can be done with multiple half-cuts. Affirm and redirect to the canonical one-cut-of-the-leftover move.
common_misconceptions: Fair share = each friend gets some, even if some get more than others. (K-stage misconception. Repair: explicit 'same amount on each plate' rule.)

Half is something you only do with pizzas, not with cookies. (Context-bound misconception. Repair: show that half works for any object — cookies, treats, biscuits, marbles. Anything can be halved if it's physical.)

If there's a leftover, it goes to the host (Plus or Lila). (Social misconception, common in classrooms with strong manners norms. Repair: 'Plus and Lila are SHARING — the host doesn't get more. The host might offer the half — but each friend gets the same amount.')
recovery_moves: Always use pre-cut paper cookies for the first half-share lesson. The visible half-line removes the cognitive load of 'how do I cut it'. Children can focus on the WHY of the half-share.
Use the body-claps analogy for half. 'One whole clap. Now half a clap.' The auditory difference makes the half concept embodied rather than abstract.
Practice the half-share habit daily for two weeks. The reflex doesn't come from one lesson; it comes from repeated practice across contexts (cookies, biscuits, marbles, fruit).

worksheet_brief.purpose: Summative evidence for B2.5. Captures both whole-quotient and half-quotient share scenarios, plus a child-explained reasoning prompt.

parts_outline.task: Two even-share scenarios. Scene A: 8 cookies, 4 friends. Scene B: 10 cookies, 5 friends. The child draws the share onto each plate and writes the per-plate count.
Two half-share scenarios. Scene A: 5 cookies, 2 friends. Scene B: 9 cookies, 2 friends. The child draws the share, splits the leftover into halves, and writes the per-plate amount as '2½' or '4½'.
Reasoning prompt: 'Why does Plus sometimes need to cut a cookie in half?' The child writes 1-2 sentences explaining the half-share rule.
